summary: Nottawasaga Island Light, one of the six Imperial Towers (lit 1858) on Georgian Bay off Collingwood, Ontario. Closed; Coast Guard property, with a volunteer society working to save it.

structures.note: Lighthouse Friends gives 85 ft; the Escarpment article gives 86 ft.

access.note: Canadian Coast Guard property; grounds and tower closed to visitors.

events.note: Tower and keeper's dwelling finished during 1856; lantern and lighting apparatus not yet installed.
Temporary light established atop the tower during 1857.
Permanent light placed in operation 30 November 1858 with a second-order Fresnel lens.
Beaches on both sides washed away and the tower's foundation was partly undermined.
Argand lamps replaced by Doty's Patent petroleum lamp (per the Escarpment article, citing Marion E. Sandell).
Steamer Mary Ward ran aground on Milligan's Reef, late 24 November 1872; keeper and son took part in the rescue.
Water level so high that waves broke against the tower in stormy weather.
Rip-rap breakwater built to protect the tower; Joseph White of Ottawa paid $950.
Red sector added to define the outer edge of the shoals between the island and Collingwood Harbour.
55 mm Diamond vapour installation on an adjustable iron stand replaced the duplex lamp (recorded in the Marine Branch report printed in 1909).
Fire badly damaged the keeper's dwelling.
Resident keepers ended after the fire; Lighthouse Friends says the light was automated at that point. The Escarpment article says fully automated in 1959.
Coast Guard officially decommissioned the light; the solar-powered light ran on its own for several more months.
Large section of the outer wall on the northeast side collapsed late in 2004 (Lighthouse Friends). The Escarpment article says the tower was struck by lightning and damaged in 2004.
$230,000 in federal funds to stabilise the tower; seven reinforcing bands fitted.
Coast Guard ceased any further maintenance of the tower (Escarpment article).
Nottawasaga Lighthouse Preservation Society incorporated as a volunteer not-for-profit.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Lighthouse Friends says the tower and dwelling were finished in 1856, with the lantern to come; the first light was placed in operation in 1858, which is the year the station record and Rowlett's directory give. Recorded as built 1856 and first lit 1858.
Lighthouse Friends gives 85 feet and the Escarpment article gives 86 feet. Both are given in the story; about 26 m is the metric equivalent of either figure.
Lighthouse Friends says the light was automated when resident keepers ended after the 1958 fire; the Escarpment article says it would be fully automated in 1959. The story gives both.

Lighthouse Friends gives Arthur George Clark 1890 to 1903 and the Escarpment article gives Captain Clark 1890 to 1902. The Escarpment article also has a 1896 photo caption calling George Collins 'Lightkeeper', which falls after the years both sources give for Collins. The story gives the Clark dates as each source states them.

notes_for_editor: Sources: Lighthouse Friends is a community site (facts only, one short quote at most); the Escarpment article is a Collingwood Museum podcast script, and its dramatised opening (the wheelbarrow scene and dialogue) is not used, only the plain fact that Jim Keith had appendicitis and reached hospital with his wife's help; the Register is the federal/provincial designation text. No pre-1900 official report was in the corpus: the 1856-1889 construction, works and keeper details rest on Lighthouse Friends' citations of Department of Marine annual reports, which I did not read. The keeper list from 1924 onward rests on Lighthouse Friends alone; Sarah Clark and Anne McNabb appear there with no stated connection to the men before them. The Escarpment article speaks of 'the 15 men' who kept the light, while Lighthouse Friends lists 18 head keepers, two of them women. Matched by position: the salary line (J. F. Burmister, $555, scan p. 177) was matched by OCR column position and checked against the page image on 2026-10-27: the Nottawasaga Island row reads J. F. Burmister, appointed May 2, 1904, $555.00 (printed p. 170). The 1909 lamp line (scan p. 83, printed p. 76) is in running text and is clean. Range: the Escarpment article gives 17 miles (27 km) without saying whether the miles are nautical, so no range_nm is recorded (the earlier 14.6 nautical miles was a conversion, now removed from the record). The 1909 report is for the fiscal year ending 31 March 1909 (the cover says printed 1909; the Sessional Paper is A. 1910). Mary Ward: only Lighthouse Friends gives the casualty figure (eight drowned) and the rescue details; a Chronicling America search for November 1872 found no matching page in the three pages I checked. The 1999 heritage date in the station record (from Wikidata) is not confirmed: the Register cites Federal Heritage Buildings Review Office Building Report 98-019 but I could not read the Directory of Federal Heritage Designations record for 8501 (page returns no detail) or the NLPS site (403). Wilfred Neil Johnston's name is in the roster as Lighthouse Friends prints it; his service runs to 1983 and nothing else is sourced, so he appears in the table only. No photos added.
